hook: If the price of coffee halves, a café owner in Seattle may barely notice. In a country where coffee brings in most of the money from exports, the same change can cut farm incomes, government budgets and school spending all at once.

options: Every step from inputs and growing through processing and sale to the consumer
The trucks and ships that carry food
A chain of farms along a river
The order of crops in a rotation
prereq.why: A commodity chain includes all the steps, not just transport.

prereq.q: Which idea describes places becoming closer in time and cost as transport improves?
prereq.why: Time-space compression is the shrinking effect of distance as travel and communication speed up.

figure.caption: A global supply chain links farms, ports, ships, warehouses and stores in different countries.

chain.cause: A country earns most of its export income from one crop, such as coffee
chain.effect: its income depends on that crop's world price

chain.cause: The world price of the crop falls sharply
chain.effect: export earnings and farm incomes drop
the government has less money for services such as schools and roads

ideas: A global supply chain links every step and place a product passes through, from farm to consumer across countries. It is more than transport.
Commodity dependence means relying on one or a few raw exports. It makes a country vulnerable to price swings; adding value and diversifying reduce it.
Food distribution is shaped by politics and conflict, trade rules, roads and storage, and income, so hunger can exist where enough food is grown.

misconception.wrong: A global supply chain is just the ships and trucks that carry food.
misconception.right: Transport is one step. A supply chain includes growing, packing, storing, processing, ripening, marketing and selling, in different countries.

summary: Global supply chains link farms, processors, shippers and stores across countries, and they are more than transport. Countries that depend on one or a few raw farm exports face price swings, and food distribution depends on politics, trade, transport and income as well as on how much is grown.
